title: Base64 Feature Against Neuron 470
takeaway: The neuron whose activations most resemble the base64 feature's shares only part of its behaviour: an activation correlation of 0.18 and a logit-weight correlation of 0.64, with most of the mass in both plots sitting off the diagonal. The paper reads this as consistent with the neuron helping represent the feature while largely doing other things, which is what it needs in order to say dictionary learning did not simply hand back an already-monosemantic base64 neuron.
walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

Two scatter plots comparing the same pair of objects, and the pair does not change between panels. On both y axes sits the [[base64-feature]] A/1/2357. On both x axes sits A/neurons/470, the [[most-correlated-neuron]] to that feature among the transformer's 512 MLP neurons.

The left panel plots activations. One point is one dataset example: how hard the neuron fired, against how hard the feature fired.

The right panel plots [[logit-weight]]s. One point is one vocabulary token: how much the neuron pushes that token's next-token logit, against how much the feature does.

One label is wrong. The left x axis reads "Feature Activations (Run B)", left over from the template that compares two dictionary learning runs; the panel title and subtitle both say the x axis here is the neuron.

### How to read it

Color is the [[base64-proxy]], a score for how base64-like a string or token is. Red is base64-looking, blue is not, and orange sits between, because that score is graded rather than binary.

The colored strips outside each axis are marginals, stacked by color, so you can read what fraction of the mass at each level is base64.

Activations are non-negative and usually exactly zero. The exact-zero row, the exact-zero column and the both-zero corner are pulled out into thin rugs and one dot, labelled "Most probability mass is at zero."

### What it shows

Left panel, [[pearson-correlation]] $0.18$. The cloud is a wide vertical smear rather than a diagonal. The feature reaches past $12$ while the neuron tops out near $6$, and the feature's strongest activations sit at middling neuron values. The y-marginal is almost all red above about $2$; the x-marginal keeps a blue majority until the neuron's top bin. The neuron does respond to base64, more than the Arabic case's neuron responds to Arabic — but not only to base64, which is [[polysemanticity]]. The thin strip where the neuron is exactly zero still carries many red points.

Right panel, correlation $0.64$. Two modes: a red ellipse of base64 tokens near $(0.17,\,0.32)$, and a much larger blue ellipse centred near the origin. The red mode is displaced up and to the right, so both raise base64 tokens. But the blue bulk is itself tilted along the diagonal, and the paper elsewhere reads that central bulk as [[weight-interference]] rather than deliberate behaviour — so a good share of $0.64$ comes from the mode it trusts least ([[feature-neuron-nonalignment]]).

terms.definition: The left panel compares how strongly two things fire on the same dataset examples. Each dot is one token position sampled from the dataset.
The right panel compares what two things do to the model's output. Each dot is one vocabulary token.
The base64 feature: feature number 2357 in dictionary learning run A/1, a 4,096-feature sparse autoencoder trained on the MLP activations of transformer A. It fires on base64-encoded strings.
Neuron 470 of transformer A's 512-unit MLP layer. The N in the title is shorthand for the paper's "neurons" slot in its identifier scheme, which keeps neurons visibly distinct from learned features.

The main one-layer transformer the paper studies, and the source of both objects plotted here. The feature is on the y axis and the neuron on the x axis, so despite the axis labels, everything in this figure comes from run A.

terms.term: Run B (in the left x-axis label)
terms.definition: A leftover from the template used for the run-A-versus-run-B universality plots, where the x axis really is a second transformer. Here it is a mislabel: the x axis is A/neurons/470, as the panel title and correlation subtitle both state.
The subtitle of each panel: a Pearson correlation between the feature's values and the neuron's values, computed over dataset examples on the left and over vocabulary tokens on the right.

terms.term: Feature Activaitons (Run A) — y axis, left panel
terms.definition: The activation of A/1/2357, i.e. the coefficient the sparse autoencoder assigns to that feature when reconstructing the MLP activation vector at a token. Spelled with a typo in the original figure.

terms.term: Feature Activations (Run B) — x axis, left panel
terms.definition: Despite the label, the post-ReLU activation of A/neurons/470 at the same token. Non-negative, like the feature's activation.

terms.term: Logit Weight (Run A) — y axis, right panel
terms.definition: For each vocabulary token, how much the feature's firing changes that token's output logit, computed by pushing the feature direction through the MLP output weights, a linearized layer norm, and the unembedding.

terms.term: Logit Weight (Run A Neuron) — x axis, right panel
terms.definition: The same quantity computed for neuron 470's direction instead of the feature's direction: how much that neuron firing changes each token's logit.

terms.term: Red points and red marginal regions
terms.definition: High base64-proxy score: dataset examples that look like base64 strings, or vocabulary tokens that occur far more often in base64 than in text generally.

terms.term: Blue points and blue marginal regions
terms.definition: Low base64-proxy score: ordinary text examples, or tokens with no base64 lean.

Middling proxy scores. The paper notes that base64-ness is a continuous distinction rather than a binary one, since any string of English letters has some chance of appearing inside a base64 blob, so the color scale has a populated middle.

The score doing the coloring: the log ratio of the probability of a string under a model of base64 (uniform over [a-zA-Z0-9+/]) to its probability under the empirical data distribution. The paper judges this proxy too broad, since hexadecimal also scores highly.

terms.term: Marginal density strips (the tall strip left of each panel, the wide strip below)
terms.definition: The one-dimensional distribution of each axis variable, drawn as stacked bands so that at each level you see the fraction of mass in each color. They are how the paper reads specificity: a strip that is red at high values means high values imply base64.

terms.term: Thin rug strips beside the scatter
terms.definition: The exact-zero row and column, drawn separately because activations pile up at zero. The narrow vertical strip holds examples where the neuron is exactly zero but the feature is positive; the narrow horizontal strip holds the reverse.
A break in the activation axes separating the exact-zero bin from the strictly positive range, so the enormous zero spike does not swamp the rest of the plot.

An annotation pointing at the single dot in the bottom-left corner, which stands for all examples where both the feature and the neuron are exactly zero. Features are sparse, so this is the overwhelming majority of tokens.
A contour drawn around the mode of base64-specific token logits, up and to the right of the origin. It marks the tokens both the feature and the neuron push up.
A contour around the main mode of ordinary tokens, centred near the origin and stretched along the diagonal. The paper's guess is that this bulk is interference rather than intended behaviour.
Reference lines marking zero logit weight on each axis. Zero is set by convention: logit weights are shifted so each vector's median is zero, since softmax is shift-invariant.

The paper's method for finding a neuron counterpart to a feature: take the neuron whose activations have the highest Pearson correlation with the feature's over roughly 40 million dataset examples. It prefers this to reading off the feature's largest coefficients in the neuron basis.
The paper's name for the large central mode of near-zero logit weights, which it hypothesizes is unwanted crosstalk forced by superposition rather than something the model wants.
A neuron that fires for a mixture of unrelated things. Neuron 470 fires on base64 but also on code, HTML labels and parts of URLs, which is why it is a poor unit of explanation on its own.

numbers.meaning: Pearson correlation between the feature's activations and neuron 470's activations, printed above the left panel. It is low because the neuron fires on plenty of non-base64 material and the feature does not track its magnitude; the paper cites this same number in the text when introducing the neuron.

Pearson correlation between the two logit-weight vectors, over vocabulary tokens, printed above the right panel. It is much higher than 0.18 because both vectors raise base64 tokens and, additionally, the large central mode of small weights is itself tilted along the diagonal.

The shared range of both activation axes on the left panel. It is shared because the panel reuses the feature-versus-feature template, so the neuron gets the same scale as the feature even though the two quantities have no common unit.
Roughly the largest feature activation reached in the scatter, on the y axis. The feature's activation scale runs well past the neuron's.
Roughly where neuron 470's activations stop in the scatter, on the x axis. Everything above about 6.5 in the bottom marginal is one merged tail bin, drawn as a uniform block.

The feature activation above which the y-marginal is essentially solid red. Below it, blue creeps in: the feature's weak activations are less reliably base64, the same pattern the paper reports for its other features.
The shared range of both logit-weight axes on the right panel. Logit weights are median-centred, so the scale straddles zero and the units are logits.
Roughly where the red base64-token mode sits: neuron weight around +0.17, feature weight around +0.32. Both are positive, so both push base64 tokens up, but the feature pushes about twice as hard.
Roughly where the blue bulk of ordinary tokens is centred: close to the origin on both axes, as expected for weights the paper reads as interference around a median of zero.
The index of the feature within run A/1. It carries no meaning beyond identity; features are numbered arbitrarily within a dictionary.
The index of the neuron within transformer A's MLP layer, between 0 and 511.
The dictionary learning run index. A/1 is the 4,096-feature run, an 8x expansion over the 512 neurons, and the run all the paper's detailed feature analyses use.
The number of neurons in the transformer's MLP layer, and so the number of candidates searched when looking for the most correlated neuron.

The number of features in run A/1, eight times the neuron count. Having more features than neurons is the point: it is what lets the decomposition pull apart directions that share neurons under superposition.
The size of the dataset sample over which the paper computes activation correlations like the 0.18 here, large enough for a rare feature to fire on a usable number of tokens.

Reported in the surrounding text, not on this figure: the Pearson correlation between the base64 proxy and the feature's activity. The paper blames the shortfall on the proxy being too broad, since hexadecimal strings score as base64 but are handled by a separate feature, A/1/3817.

The comparison values from the matching figure for the Arabic script feature and its most correlated neuron. Base64's 0.18 and 0.64 are both higher, which is why the paper says this neuron does notably respond to base64 rather than dismissing it outright.

The activation and logit-weight correlations between A/1/2357 and its counterpart feature B/1/2165 in a second transformer, from the universality figure. They set the scale for what a genuine match looks like, and 0.18 falls far short of it.
